source_spans.locator: Nature 401, published pp.584-585, Abstract and opening rationale: superimposed face/house stimuli; independently localized face-, place/house-, and motion-sensitive regions; central test of whether a task-relevant attribute carries enhancement to task-irrelevant attributes of the same object

Nature 401, published p.585, Experiment 1: seven subjects; blocked crossing of face-moving versus house-moving stimuli with attend-face, attend-house, and attend-motion tasks; direct preferred-attribute enhancement plus greater response to the task-irrelevant attribute of the selected object

Nature 401, published p.586, Experiment 2: four subjects; event-related random intermix of moving-face/static-house and moving-house/static-face trials; motion-direction versus stationary-position repetition tasks; form identity unpredictable and never task relevant; same-object irrelevant-form enhancement remains

Nature 401, published p.586, interpretation and limits: event-related result rejects strategic use of the irrelevant dimension; objects are not claimed to be the only possible units; task-relevant responses can exceed same-object task-irrelevant responses; biased-competition account is offered as an interpretation rather than a uniquely established mechanism

Nature 401, published pp.586-587, Methods: seven normal young adults in Experiment 1 and four in Experiment 2; task timing, fixation/repetition-detection instructions, independent ROI localization, and Experiment 2 peak-response measure at 4-6 s after stimulus onset

institutions: MIT Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences

conditions: a face and a house are transparently superimposed at the same retinal location, with one object moving and the other stationary
Experiment 1 uses blocked instructions to monitor face identity, house identity, or motion direction
Experiment 2 randomly intermixes which object moves and requires monitoring only motion direction or the position of the stationary object, so face/house form is unpredictable and task irrelevant
population: seven normal young adults in Experiment 1 and four normal young adults in Experiment 2
substrate: independently localized fusiform face-selective, parahippocampal place/house-selective, and MT/MST motion-selective regions
task: detect consecutive repetitions of the instructed visual attribute in Experiment 1
detect consecutive repetitions of motion direction or stationary-object position in separate event-related scans in Experiment 2
temporal_scope: Experiment 1 uses 28-s task blocks with 675-ms stimulus presentations separated by 725-ms inter-trial intervals
Experiment 2 uses 375-ms stimulus presentations in randomized event-related trials; regional response magnitude is measured from the 4-6 s post-stimulus peak

nodes.description: assignment of form identity and motion or position attributes to each of the two superimposed visual objects
instruction specifying which visual dimension must be monitored for consecutive repetitions
the superimposed object that carries the currently task-relevant visual dimension on a block or trial
a visual attribute of the selected object that is not required for the current task, such as face or house form during the motion or position tasks
the corresponding visual attribute belonging to the other superimposed object
percent magnetic-resonance signal change in independently localized face-, place/house-, or motion-selective regions
Experiment 1 blocked fMRI comparison crossing which object moves with face, house, or motion monitoring instructions
Experiment 2 randomized event-related fMRI comparison in which moving versus stationary object identity is unpredictable and only motion direction or stationary position is task relevant

relations.description: in Experiment 1, each selective region shows a larger response when its preferred visual attribute is directly task relevant than when another attribute of the same display is selected
the instructed dimension determines which superimposed object carries the task-relevant attribute, given the source-defined binding of form with motion or position
the neural representation of a task-irrelevant attribute is greater when that attribute belongs to the selected object than when it belongs to the other object
the blocked Experiment 1 procedure measures direct task-relevant enhancement and same-object enhancement of task-irrelevant attributes

the randomized Experiment 2 procedure tests the same-object enhancement when form identity is unpredictable and never task relevant, removing strategic use of the irrelevant dimension as an explanation
